definition: Preachy means pushing moral advice or lessons in a smug, tiresome way — lecturing an audience on right and wrong when nobody asked for the sermon.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word preachy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know preachy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The reviews praised the documentary's research but called its narration preachy: every scene ended with the voice-over telling viewers exactly what to feel about it.
Didactic is milder than preachy: a didactic story merely sets out to teach its lesson, while a preachy one keeps hammering the moral long after everyone has heard it.
Sanctimonious goes further than preachy: the preachy narrator at least cares about the advice itself, while a sanctimonious one has moved on to advertising their own virtue.
Moralizing means passing judgment on right and wrong at every opportunity; preachy adds the audience's fatigue — the lecture keeps going after it has worn out its welcome.

Sanctimonious means making a show of one's own moral superiority; a sanctimonious speaker performs virtue, while a preachy one pushes advice — you can be preachy out of honest concern and still be tiresome.
Didactic means designed to teach a lesson — a didactic fable is simply doing its job; preachy is didactic gone wrong, the lesson delivered with a wagging finger nobody invited.
making its point lightly, without insisting
offering no verdict on anyone's choices

Preachy means pushing moral advice or lessons in a smug, tiresome way — lecturing an audience on right and wrong when nobody asked for the sermon.
Halfway through the novel the author turns preachy: the plot stops dead so a wise grandmother can deliver two full pages on gratitude, and the story never quite recovers its footing.
The lesson itself may be perfectly sound — gratitude is a fine thing — but preachy is a complaint about delivery: moral instruction pressed on an audience that came for a story, not a sermon.
The suffix -y turns the verb preach into an adjective, 'characterized by preaching.'
Preachy is a critic's word — aim it at tone, never at content: a book can argue hard for honesty without being preachy, and a preachy one can still be right.
It pairs naturally with laudatory, taught in this same unit: one voice drowns you in praise, the other in advice.

The gardening show's first two seasons were beloved for their modesty: a trowel, a row of beans, no philosophy.
Season three opened with a new host and a new tone.
Viewers who tuned in to learn about aphids now received, with every episode, a sermon — on patience, on gratitude, on the moral instruction hidden in compost.
Letters to the network used the same word again and again: preachy.
One viewer wrote, 'I agreed with every lesson and still could not bear being taught it twice a week.' The producers quietly returned the show to beans and aphids, and the letters stopped.
